concept.name: Distributed ledger
concept.definition: A distributed ledger is a database that is replicated, shared and synchronized across multiple nodes or institutions, with updates agreed through a consensus process rather than written by a single central administrator.
concept.intuition: Instead of one bank keeping the master copy of the books, every participant keeps an identical copy and they all agree on each new entry.
concept.mechanics: Each node holds a copy of the ledger; new records are propagated through the peer-to-peer network and accepted only if they satisfy the protocol's validation and consensus rules. A blockchain is one specific form of distributed ledger that orders records in cryptographically chained blocks, but DLT also includes non-block structures (e.g. DAGs, permissioned ledgers).
concept.failure_modes: If the consensus layer or validator set is compromised or centralized in practice, the ledger can be censored or rewritten despite nominal distribution; poor network connectivity can partition the ledger into divergent views.
concept.misconceptions: 'Distributed ledger' and 'blockchain' are not synonyms — all blockchains are DLT, but distributed ledgers need not organize data in blocks or be public. Distribution of copies does not by itself guarantee distribution of control.
concept.example: Ethereum's ledger of accounts and smart-contract state is stored and updated by every node in the network, so two independent nodes reading the same finalized block compute the same balances without trusting each other.
